title: NY State Assembly · District 73
area: Manhattan's East Side, including the Upper East Side, Midtown East and parts of the Flatiron District.

context.text: Open seat: incumbent Alex Bores (D) is not seeking re-election to the Assembly; he ran for the U.S. House in New York's 12th Congressional District and lost in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary. Vanessa Aronson (D, WFP) is unopposed on the November ballot; she advanced from the Democratic and Working Families Party lines without a primary after her only would-be opponents withdrew — Nathaniel Gavronsky (Block Mamdani Party) withdrew, and Republican David Casavis withdrew before the canceled Republican primary.

candidates.name: Vanessa Aronson
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the Democratic and Working Families Party lines without opposition after other candidates withdrew; unopposed in the general election.

summary.text: Vanessa Aronson is the Democratic and Working Families Party nominee for the open NY State Assembly District 73 seat, running unopposed. She is a former U.S. Foreign Service officer and New York City public-school teacher who most recently worked at the ASPCA, and she previously ran unsuccessfully for New York City Council District 4 in 2017 and 2025. She is seeking the seat held by Alex Bores, who is running for Congress.

background.text: In a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey, she described growing up in a middle-class family, the daughter of a school nurse and a computer systems analyst, and said her father died suddenly when she was nine.

Earned a B.A. in political science from the University of Chicago, an M.A. in teaching from the Relay Graduate School of Education, and an M.P.P. in political advocacy and leadership from the Harvard Kennedy School.

Worked as a U.S. Department of State foreign service officer, including as vice consul at the U.S. Consulate General in Ho Chi Minh City and as a food security officer in the Bureau of International Organization Affairs. Her campaign website says she spent a decade as a Foreign Service Officer.
Worked as a math and science teacher in New York City public schools and co-founded Aronson Concierge Vacations; her campaign website also says she advised the president of Hunter College.
According to her campaign website, most recently served as Senior Director of Strategy at the ASPCA.

Describes herself as a former Community Board 8 member, former president of the Lexington Democratic Club, New York County Judicial Delegate and Democratic County Committee member, and former co-chair of the Tikkun Olam Committee at Park Avenue Synagogue.
Ran in the 2017 Democratic primary for New York City Council District 4, receiving 6.84% of the vote (746 votes) in a primary won by Keith Powers.
Placed second in the 2025 Democratic primary for New York City Council District 4, losing to Virginia Maloney in the final round of ranked-choice voting, 53.1% to 46.9%.

Filed in September 2025 to run for Assembly District 73 in case Alex Bores, the incumbent, ran for Congress; as of April 2026 City & State reported she was the only Democrat to file petitions, so no Democratic primary was held. Lives on the Upper East Side with her husband and two children, according to her campaign website.

priorities.text: Reducing the influence of lobbyists, particularly for business and real-estate interests, on government decisions.
Expanding oversight of police surveillance technology.
Continued legal representation for immigrants facing deportation proceedings.

positions.summary: In a March 2026 club questionnaire, said she supports the New York for All Act, which would limit state and local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
positions.quote: I support the New York For All Act, which would prohibit state and local resources from being used to further federal immigration enforcement, limit local cooperation with ICE, and protect immigrant New Yorkers’ basic rights

positions.summary: In a March 2026 club questionnaire, answered yes when asked whether she supports the unrestricted right to reproductive care and abortion.
In a March 2026 club questionnaire, said New York cannot afford to cut Medicaid and other programs to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
positions.quote: We cannot afford to cut funding to important programs like SNAP, Medicaid, special education services, and more to pay for tax breaks for the ultra-wealthy.

candidates.researchNotes: Aronson has not held elected office, so there is no official voting or bill-sponsorship record. Her only completed Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey dates to her 2017 City Council run; no updated 2026 Assembly campaign website could be reached (vanessataronson.com did not resolve), so her documented priorities and the one mapped issue position reflect that earlier survey rather than confirmed current statements for this race.
